Text:
Introns are removed by three splicing mechanisms, each tied to its own class of precursor RNA — match the machinery to the substrate:

{{c2::tRNA::which precursor RNA}} precursors → {{c1::a splicing endonuclease and a splicing ligase::protein enzymes / the RNA itself / a spliceosome}}

some {{c2::rRNA::which precursor RNA}} precursors → {{c1::the RNA itself, autocatalytically — no protein enzyme::protein enzymes / the RNA itself / a spliceosome}}

nuclear {{c2::pre-mRNA (hnRNA)::which precursor RNA}} → {{c1::a spliceosome::protein enzymes / the RNA itself / a spliceosome}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: all three mechanisms cut the intron out and rejoin the flanking RNA — what differs is who does the chemistry: dedicated protein enzymes, the RNA itself, or a ribonucleoprotein particle.

Cue: 'endo-nuclease' cuts within the chain, 'ligase' ties the pieces back together, 'auto-catalytic' means the RNA catalyzes its own excision.

Pitfall: only SOME rRNA precursors self-splice, and nuclear pre-mRNA introns never self-splice — they need the spliceosome.

The introns of tRNA precursors are excised by precise endonucleolytic cleavage and ligation reactions catalyzed by special splicing endonuclease and ligase activities.' | p294: '2. The introns of some rRNA precursors are removed autocatalytically in a unique reaction mediated by the RNA molecule itself. No protein enzymatic activity is involved in this splicing process.' | p294: '3. The introns of nuclear pre-mRNAs (hnRNAs) are removed in two-step reactions carried out by complex ribonucleoprotein particles called splicesomes.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p296: 'However, the introns are not excised by simple splicing nucleases and ligases or autocatalytically, and no guanosine cofactor is required. Instead, nuclear pre-mRNA splicing is carried out by complex RNA–protein structures called spliceosomes.'

Text: The spliceosomes that remove introns from pre-mRNA are particles built of {{c1::RNA and protein::two macromolecule classes}}; they work inside the {{c2::nucleus::cell compartment}} of eukaryotic cells and excise each intron in a {{c3::two::number of steps}}-step reaction.
Back Extra:
Why: splicing is finished before export — intron sequences are excised from transcripts in the nucleus, and only the spliced mRNA travels to the cytoplasm for translation.

Distinguish: tRNA introns are cut out by two dedicated protein enzymes and some rRNA introns cut themselves out; only nuclear pre-mRNA introns need the spliceosome.

Text: Across the introns of nuclear genes, the only completely conserved sequences are the two dinucleotides at the intron's ends, written for the DNA nontemplate strand as exon-{{c1::GT::5′ dinucleotide}}……{{c1::AG::3′ dinucleotide}}-exon.
Back Extra:
Meaning: the nontemplate strand reads like the RNA transcript with T in place of U, so in the pre-mRNA the intron begins GU and ends AG.

Pitfall: 'completely conserved' applies only to the two end dinucleotides — the rest of each junction is a consensus with percentage frequencies, and the body of an intron is barely conserved at all (introns collect mutations far faster than exons).

Distinguish: tRNA genes and the protein-coding genes of mitochondria and chloroplasts have different junctions and use different splicing mechanisms.

Text:
Yeast tRNA precursor splicing (stage I): a {{c1::nuclear membrane-bound::its location}} splicing endonuclease makes {{c2::two::how many}} cuts, precisely at the {{c2::ends::which part}} of the intron.

Yeast tRNA precursor splicing (stage II): a splicing ligase joins {{c3::both halves of the tRNA::what it joins}}, yielding the mature tRNA.
Back Extra:
Ex: the pathway was worked out in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, with in-vitro splicing systems and temperature-sensitive splicing mutants.

Cue: cut twice, then tie once — nuclease first, ligase second; the intron falls out between the two cuts, and the ligase joins the tRNA halves, not the intron.

Distinguish: unlike a self-splicing rRNA intron (the RNA itself) or a pre-mRNA intron (a spliceosome), the tRNA intron is removed by two dedicated protein enzymes.

Then, in stage II, a splicing ligase joins the two halves of the tRNA to produce the mature form of the tRNA molecule.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p295: 'The tRNA precursor splicing reaction has been worked out in detail in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Both in vitro splicing systems and temperature-sensitive splicing mutants have been used to analyze the tRNA splicing mechanism in S. cerevisiae.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p294: marks 65–67 (the three mechanisms)

Isaacs numbers the three intron-splicing mechanisms type 1, 2 and 3 — name the precursor RNA each type acts on:

Type 1 splicing → introns of {{c1::tRNA::which precursor RNA}} precursors

Text: The specificity of type 1 (tRNA-precursor) splicing resides in the precursor's conserved {{c1::three-dimensional structure::3-D structure or nucleotide sequence}} — Isaacs' one-word term for such splicing is '{{c1::shape}} driven'. He applies the same term to {{c2::type 2 (self-splicing rRNA precursors)::type 2 or type 3}}; the remaining type reads sequence signals instead.
Back Extra:
Why: the tRNA cuts and ligation are specified by conserved three-dimensional features of the precursor, not by its nucleotide sequences per se — the enzymes read a fold, not a motif.

Distinguish: type 3 (spliceosomal) splicing is the sequence-read one — the GU…AG ends and the branch-point consensus are recognized by snRNPs, the 5′ site by base-pairing with U1 snRNA.

Pitfall: 'shape driven' for type 2 means the self-splicing activity depends on the secondary structure of the intron (or of the whole precursor), which folds to form its own active center.

Text: The first self-splicing intron was found in {{c1::1982::year}} by {{c1::Thomas Cech::researcher}} and coworkers, in the rRNA precursor of {{c2::Tetrahymena thermophila::organism}}; the discovery of {{c3::catalytic RNAs::what}} later earned him and Sidney Altman a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Back Extra:
Why: the finding was startling because covalent bonds were assumed to be altered only by enzymes, and enzymes were assumed to be proteins — yet the intron was excised with no protein catalytic activity at all, so the catalysis is intrinsic to the RNA molecule itself.

Cue: 'catalytic RNA' is the general term; 'self-splicing' or 'autocatalytic' names what the Tetrahymena intron does. The Nobel came in 1989, seven years after the discovery.

Text: Type 2 splicing (the self-splicing Tetrahymena rRNA intron) uses no protein and no external energy source, but it does need one cofactor — a {{c1::guanine::which base}} nucleoside or nucleotide with a free {{c1::3′-OH::which reactive group}} — plus {{c2::a monovalent cation and a divalent cation::which ions}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the G requirement is absolute — no other base can be substituted — but the phosphates are irrelevant: GTP, GDP, GMP or free guanosine all work.

Why: the precursor RNA folds to form an active center in which the guanosine-3′-OH cofactor binds — proof that catalytic sites are not restricted to proteins.

Cue: Isaacs' bullets for type 2 — no protein enzymatic activity; requires guanosine with 3′-OH; two phosphoester bond transfers; reversible if products not degraded.

Text: In type 2 splicing (self-splicing) the intron is excised by {{c1::two::how many}} phosphoester bond transfers, after which the excised intron can {{c2::circularize::what it does}} by one more transfer. Because every step is a bond transfer with {{c3::no bonds lost or gained::net bond change}}, the reaction needs {{c3::no::no / an}} external energy source.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: transfer 1 — the phosphoester bond at the exon 1–intron junction moves onto the guanosine's 3′-OH, cutting exon 1 free; transfer 2 — the bond at the intron–exon 2 junction moves onto the 3′ end of exon 1, joining the two exons; a third, internal transfer then closes the excised intron into a circle.

Distinguish: spliceosomal (type 3) splicing is also two steps, but its first step requires ATP hydrolysis and no guanosine.

Why: the circularization of the excised intron on its own shows that the self-splicing activity resides primarily, if not entirely, within the intron itself.

Text: The phosphoester bond transfers of self-splicing are potentially {{c1::reversible::reversible or irreversible}}, so what drives type 2 splicing forward in the cell is rapid {{c1::degradation::fate}} of the excised intron or {{c1::export to the cytoplasm::fate}} of the spliced rRNA.
Back Extra:
Why: with no bonds lost or gained there is nothing to make the forward direction favorable on its own, so the cell tips the balance by taking the products away — Isaacs' phrasing: 'reversible if products not degraded'.

Cue: reversible, intramolecular, and no external energy source — the three thermodynamic quirks of self-splicing.

Text: Because a self-splicing reaction is {{c1::intramolecular::intra- or intermolecular}}, its rate is {{c1::not::not / strongly}} dependent on concentration; and while a protein enzyme shows {{c2::trans::cis or trans}} catalytic activity, the catalytic RNA shows only {{c2::cis::cis or trans}} catalytic activity.
Back Extra:
Meaning: cis = acting on the very molecule it is part of; trans = acting on separate substrate molecules, as enzymes do.

Why: catalytic sites are not restricted to proteins — but a self-splicing RNA catalyzes only its own excision, so it is not an enzyme in the usual sense.

Cue: some scientists read autocatalytic RNA splicing as a relic of an early RNA-based world.

Text: Nuclear pre-mRNA introns come out in two steps, like tRNA and Tetrahymena rRNA introns, but a spliceosome does the chemistry: the first step requires the hydrolysis of {{c1::ATP::energy source}}, and a {{c2::guanosine::which cofactor}} cofactor is not required.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the pre-mRNA intron is excised neither by simple splicing nucleases and ligases (type 1) nor autocatalytically (type 2); and where self-splicing needs no external energy but an obligatory guanosine, the spliceosome needs ATP but no guanosine.

Why: the ATP is spent on the complete spliceosome during the first cleavage, at the 5′ splice site.

Text:
Spliceosome assembly on a nuclear pre-mRNA — which snRNP binds where, in order of arrival:

{{c2::U1::which snRNP}} snRNP → binds the {{c1::5′ splice site::which site}} (first)

{{c2::U2::which snRNP}} snRNP → binds the {{c1::branch-point consensus (with the conserved A)::which site}} (second)

{{c2::U5::which snRNP}} snRNP → binds the {{c1::3′ splice site::which site}} (third)

{{c2::U4/U6::which snRNP}} snRNP → joins the complex, completing the spliceosome (last)
Back Extra:
Mechanism: U1 recognizes the 5′ splice site by base-pairing between the site's consensus and a complementary sequence near the 5′ end of U1 snRNA; the U2 site is the consensus containing the A that becomes the lariat branch point.

Pitfall: U1 must be bound at the 5′ site before the first cleavage can happen, and the moment the 5′ site is cut U4 leaves the complex.

Cue: 1 – 2 – 5, then the 4/6 pair.

Pitfall: U1 also leaves at the step-1 cleavage (its job, marking the 5′ site, is done), so only U2, U5 and U6 stay with the intron to the end — but if asked for the one snRNA released at step 1, answer U4.

Text: Nuclear pre-mRNA splicing (step 2): the {{c1::3′::5′ or 3′}} splice site is cleaved and the two exons are joined by a normal 5′→3′ {{c1::phosphodiester::bond type}} linkage; the lariat-shaped intron is released together with snRNPs {{c2::U2, U5 and U6::which three}}, and the spliced mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm for translation.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: step 1's linkage was the odd one — the intron's 5′ G onto the 2′ carbon of an A — whereas step 2's is the ordinary backbone bond of RNA.

Why: only after both steps is the mRNA ready for export to the cytoplasm and translation on ribosomes; introns are excised in the nucleus and never travel with the message.

Pitfall: U4 is already gone (released at step 1's cleavage), which is why it is not among the snRNPs that leave with the lariat.

Text: In nuclear pre-mRNA splicing the {{c1::branch point::term}} is {{c2::a conserved A near the intron's 3′ end}} — the residue whose 2′ carbon receives the intron's 5′ end, making the looped intermediate called a {{c3::lariat::term for the shape}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the intron's 5′ end bonds to the A's 2′ carbon while the A's 3′ side keeps running on into the rest of the intron, so the excised intron is a loop with a tail — a lasso shape, hence 'lariat'.

Distinguish: the 5′ and 3′ splice sites are the intron's ends (GU…AG); the branch point is an interior residue near the 3′ end.

Cue: in Isaacs' shorthand GT…TACTAAC…AG, the branch-point A is the sixth base of TACTAAC — the A he prints in red.

Text: Isaacs' shorthand for a nuclear intron on the nontemplate DNA strand is exon-GT…{{c1::TACTAAC::7-base branch-point consensus}}…AG-exon — the interior consensus that carries the branch-point A of the lariat.
Back Extra:
Meaning: the consensus lies inside the intron, upstream of the 3′ AG; its marked A — the sixth base, TACTA-A-C — is the residue whose 2′ carbon receives the intron's 5′ G to form the lariat.

Distinguish: GT and AG are the invariant intron ends; TACTAAC marks the branch point, an interior residue 'near the 3′ end of the intron'.

Pitfall: written for the nontemplate DNA strand — in the RNA it reads GU…UACUAAC…AG.

Text: In the splice-junction consensus of nuclear genes (for example G100 T100 opening the intron), a numerical subscript gives the {{c1::percentage frequency::what the number means}} of the base at its position, so a subscript of 100 means the base is {{c1::always::how often}} present; the run of six positions a little upstream of the 3′-end AG is filled by {{c2::pyrimidines (Py)::which base class}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: N = any of the four standard nucleotides; Py = either pyrimidine (C or T). The full nuclear-gene consensus on the nontemplate strand, subscripts written as plain numbers after each base: exon A64 G73 | intron G100 T100 A68 A68 G84 T63 ………… 6Py(74–87) N C65 A100 G100 | exon N.

Cue: the exon's last two bases are usually A-G as well, so a typical 5′ junction reads …AG|GTAAGT…, with only the GT invariant.

Distinguish: the junctions differ for tRNA genes and for the protein-coding genes of mitochondria and chloroplasts, whose transcripts use different splicing mechanisms.

Text: {{c1::Alternative splicing::process}} of a pre-mRNA is {{c2::removing its introns in more than one pattern}}, which yields mRNAs that encode {{c3::different but related::how the products compare}} polypeptides — so one gene can encode more than one product.
Back Extra:
Why: introns thereby increase the coding potential of the entire genome — one gene, several related proteins.

Cue: under 'mRNA processing' Isaacs files splicing as two items — removal of introns, and alternative splicing.

Text: For a protein-coding gene, RNA splicing must join the exons with accuracy to {{c1::the single nucleotide::what tolerance}}, because the join decides whether the {{c2::codons::which units}} in every exon distal to the intron are read correctly.
Back Extra:
Why: shift the join by even one nucleotide and every codon downstream of the intron is translated wrongly, so the polypeptide's amino acid sequence downstream of the join is wrong.

Pitfall: 'distal to the intron' means the exons downstream of it — the ones whose codons a mis-join would throw off.

Cue: single-nucleotide precision is why the junction signals matter — the invariant GU…AG ends and the consensus around them.

Text: In the processing of a eukaryotic transcript, {{c1::splicing::process}} is {{c2::removing introns and joining the remaining RNA}}; it is finished in the nucleus, before the transcript is exported to the cytoplasm.
Back Extra:
Cue: on Isaacs' mRNA-processing list, splicing = 'removal of introns' (plus alternative splicing).

Why: introns are noncoding, so only after they are cut out and the remaining sequences joined is the message ready for export and translation on ribosomes.
